concepts: Evaluation of limits using series expansion
Distance between a curve and its inverse (symmetry about $y=x$)
questions.question: Let $k$ be a real constant defined by $k=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\cos(xe^{-x})-\cos(xe^{x})}{2x^3}$. Consider two non-intersecting curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ in the $xy$-plane defined by $C_1:y=e^x+2k$ and $C_2:y=\ln(x-2k)$ (for $x>2k$). If $d$ is the minimum distance between the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$, then $d$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $C_1$ and $C_2$ are inverse functions, so they are mirror images in $y=x$ and the closest points have tangents parallel to $y=x$.
solution: These are inverse functions, so they are symmetric with respect to the line $y=x$.
The minimum distance $d$ occurs along the common normal, which has slope $-1$.
On $C_1$ the closest point $P(x_1,y_1)$ is where the tangent is parallel to $y=x$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x_1}=1\Rightarrow x_1=0\Rightarrow P(0,3)$.
On $C_2$ the closest point $Q(x_2,y_2)$ is where $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{x_2-2}=1\Rightarrow x_2=3\Rightarrow Q(3,0)$.
The segment $PQ$ has slope $-1$, so it is perpendicular to both tangents.

alternate_solutions.idea: Product-to-sum for $k$, and reflection: $d$ is twice the distance from $C_1$ to the line $y=x$.
solution: $\cos A-\cos B=-2\sin\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{A-B}{2}$ with $A=xe^{-x}$, $B=xe^{x}$ gives $\frac{A+B}{2}=x\cosh x$ and $\frac{A-B}{2}=-x\sinh x$.
So the numerator is $2\sin(x\cosh x)\sin(x\sinh x)$ and $k=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(x\cosh x)\sin(x\sinh x)}{x^3}$.
As $x\to0$: $\sin(x\cosh x)\sim x$ and $\sin(x\sinh x)\sim x^2$, hence $k=1$.
$C_2$ is the mirror image of $C_1$ in $y=x$, so the shortest distance between them is $2\times$ (shortest distance from $C_1$ to the line $x-y=0$).
Distance of $(x,e^x+2)$ from $x-y=0$ is $\frac{e^x+2-x}{\sqrt2}$ (positive, since $e^x\ge x+1$).
Let $\varphi(x)=e^x-x+2$: $\varphi'(x)=e^x-1=0$ at $x=0$ and $\varphi''>0$, so the minimum is $\varphi(0)=3$.

useful_results: The graph of $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x)$ are mirror images in $y=x$; if the curve does not meet $y=x$, the minimum distance between them is $2\times\min\frac{|f(x)-x|}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2\,\min|f(x)-x|$.
Closest points of a curve to a line are where the tangent is parallel to that line (equal slopes), here $e^{x}=1$.
$\cos A-\cos B=-2\sin\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{A-B}{2}$ turns a difference of cosines with a cancelling $x^2$ term into a product of two small sines (orders $x\cdot x^2$).
Instance: $e^x\ge x+1$ gives $\min(e^x+2-x)=3$ at $x=0$, so $d=\sqrt2\cdot3=3\sqrt2$.

concepts: Definite integral of greatest integer function using the King property
questions.question: If $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$, then the value of the definite integral $I=\int_0^{\pi}\left([2\sin2x]+[2\cos2x]\right)dx$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $[t]+[-t]=-1$ for non-integer $t$, so pair $x$ with its reflection until the argument of the integrand turns odd.
solution: $[t]+[-t]=-1$ when $t$ is not an integer, and $2\sin2x$ is an integer only at finitely many points of $(0,\frac{\pi}{2})$. So the integrand is $-1$ almost everywhere.
Apply the same property to $I_2$ with $2a=\pi$: $I_2=\int_0^{\pi/2}\left([2\cos2x]+[2\cos(2(\pi-x))]\right)dx=2\int_0^{\pi/2}[2\cos2x]\,dx$, because $\cos(2\pi-2x)=\cos2x$.
Since $2\cos2x$ is not an integer almost everywhere on $(0,\frac{\pi}{4})$, the integrand is $-1$: $I_2=2\int_0^{\pi/4}(-1)\,dx=-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $\theta=2x$ so the integrand lives on a full period, then use the half-period shift $\theta\to\theta+\pi$ that changes the sign of sine and cosine.
solution: The integrand $[2\sin\theta]$ has period $2\pi$, and $\sin(\theta+\pi)=-\sin\theta$. So $\int_0^{2\pi}[2\sin\theta]\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi}\left([2\sin\theta]+[2\sin(\theta+\pi)]\right)d\theta=\int_0^{\pi}\left([2\sin\theta]+[-2\sin\theta]\right)d\theta$.
Because $[t]+[-t]=-1$ except at integers, this equals $\int_0^{\pi}(-1)\,d\theta=-\pi$.

useful_results: For non-integer $t$: $[t]+[-t]=-1$ and $\{t\}+\{-t\}=1$. If $g(x)+g(c-x)=0$ (or the integrand is odd about the midpoint), then $\int_a^b[g]\,dx=-\frac{b-a}{2}$ over that range, up to a set of measure zero.
Over a full period, $\sin$ and $\cos$ change sign under a half-period shift, so $\int_0^{T}[k\sin\theta]\,d\theta=-\frac{T}{2}$ whenever $k\sin\theta$ is not an integer almost everywhere.
General form: $\int_0^{n\pi}[a\sin x]\,dx=-\frac{n\pi}{2}$ and $\int_0^{2n\pi}[a\cos x]\,dx=-n\pi$ for any real $a\neq0$.
Instance: $\int_0^{\pi}[2\sin2x]\,dx=\int_0^{\pi}[2\cos2x]\,dx=-\frac{\pi}{2}$.

concepts: Indefinite integration: partial fractions
Angle between two curves
questions.question: Let $f:(1,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\int\frac{x^2+1}{x^4-x^2}\,dx$ satisfying the condition $f(2)=\frac12-\ln3$. Consider the curves $C_1:y=f(x)$ and $C_2:y=\frac1x-\ln(x+1)$. If the acute angle of intersection between the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ is $\theta$, then $\theta$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: $f(2)$ equals the value of $C_2$ at $x=2$, so the curves meet at $x=2$ and only the two slopes are needed.
solution: Since $1+m_1m_2=\frac{109}{144}>0$ the angle is acute, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{144}{109}\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The initial condition already gives the common point, and the difference of the two curves has derivative $\frac1{x-1}>0$, so no integration is needed at all.
solution: $C_2$ at $x=2$ has $y=\frac12-\ln3$, which is exactly the given $f(2)$, so $(2,\frac12-\ln3)$ lies on both curves.
So $h$ is strictly increasing and has at most one zero; $h(2)=0$, hence $x=2$ is the only intersection.
Slopes at $x=2$ come straight from the integrand and from $g'$: $m_1=\frac{5}{12}$, $m_2=-\frac{7}{12}$.
The tangents have inclinations $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac5{12}$ above and $\beta=\tan^{-1}\frac7{12}$ below the $x$-axis, so the angle between them is $\alpha+\beta$ ($<\frac\pi2$).

useful_results: $f(x)=\int f'(x)dx$ with a given value $f(a)$: if that value matches another curve at $x=a$, the point is a common point and no antiderivative is needed for slopes.
Angle between curves at a common point: $\tan\theta=\left|\frac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$; the angle is acute iff $1+m_1m_2>0$. If $m_1>0>m_2$, $\theta=\tan^{-1}m_1+\tan^{-1}|m_2|$.
$\frac{x^2+1}{x^2(x^2-1)}=\frac{2}{x^2-1}-\frac1{x^2}$ and $\int\frac{2}{x^2-1}dx=\ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+1}\right|$.
Two curves $y=f$, $y=g$ meet only where $h=f-g$ vanishes; if $h'$ has a fixed sign, the meeting point is unique.

concepts: Limit of a sum as a definite integral and trigonometric substitution
questions.question: Let $L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{n^6-k^6+n^2k^2(n^2-k^2)}}$. Then the value of $L$ is
questions.key_idea: The radicand factors as $(n^2-k^2)(n^2+k^2)^2$, which turns the sum into a Riemann sum of $\frac{1}{(1+x^2)\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: One direct substitution $t=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ (that is, $t=\tan\theta$) removes the root and the $\sin\theta$ step, and the standard formula confirms the value.
solution: After the factorisation, $L=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ (as in the main solution).
Check with the standard result $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\theta}{a+b\sin^2\theta}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{a(a+b)}}$ for $a=b=1$: $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt2}$.

useful_results: Sums with $n^2$ in the numerator and a sixth-degree radicand are Riemann sums: divide by $n^3$ and put $x=\frac kn$ to get $\frac1n\sum f\left(\frac kn\right)\to\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$.
$\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\theta}{a+b\sin^2\theta}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{a(a+b)}}$ for $a>0,\ a+b>0$ (check: $a=1,b=0$ gives $\frac\pi2$).
$\int\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)\sqrt{1-x^2}}$: $x=\sin\theta$ followed by $t=\tan\theta$ is the standard route for $\frac{1}{(p+qx^2)\sqrt{1-x^2}}$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Integration by substitution and differential relation
Common tangent to two curves
questions.question: Let $f:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuously differentiable function satisfying the differential relation $df(x)=\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ for all $x\in(0,1)$. Suppose the curve $y=f(x)$ passes through the point $\left(\frac12,-\sqrt3\right)$ and is denoted by $C_1$. Let $C_2$ be the curve defined by the equation $x^2=\frac32y$. If a line $L$ is a common tangent to both the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$, touching $C_1$ at the point $P$ and $C_2$ at the point $Q$, then which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
options: One possible equation of the common tangent line $L$ is $2\sqrt2x-y-3=0$
The length of the line segment $PQ$ is $3\sqrt2$
The area of the triangle formed by the line $L$ with the coordinate axes is $\frac{9}{2\sqrt2}$
questions.key_idea: A tangent of slope $m$ to $x^2=\frac32y$ has $y$-intercept $-\frac{3m^2}{8}$, which pins down the point of contact on $C_1$.
solution: Slope of the tangent to $C_1$: $y'=\frac{1}{x^2\sqrt{1-x^2}}$. For $C_2$: $y=\frac23x^2\Rightarrow y'=\frac43x$.

A line of slope $m$ touching $C_2$ at $x_2=\frac{3m}{4}$ has $y$-intercept $-\frac{3m^2}{8}$, so the tangent to $C_1$ at $x_1$ (slope $m$) must have the same intercept. This condition is satisfied by $x_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ (and by one more value $x_1\approx0.903$, a second common tangent not used in the options).
Choosing $x_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ gives the slope $m=2\sqrt2$ and the point $P\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},-1\right)$.
For $C_2$, put the slope $\frac43x_2=2\sqrt2$: $x_2=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}$, which corresponds to the point $Q\left(\frac{3\sqrt2}{2},3\right)$.
Substituting $Q$ in the line: $2\sqrt2\left(\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\right)-3-3=0$, which confirms that it is a valid common tangent.
The intercepts of the line $2\sqrt2x-y=3$ are $\left(\frac{3}{2\sqrt2},0\right)$ and $(0,-3)$.
Area of the triangle with the axes $=\frac12\cdot\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}\cdot|-3|=\frac{9}{4\sqrt2}\neq\frac{9}{2\sqrt2}$. Statement (D) is false.
questions.correction_note: PDF said 'Choosing x1 = 1/sqrt2' without showing why this point gives a common tangent, did not give the verdicts on (A) and (D), and the question actually has two common tangents: the condition c = -3m^2/8 has roots x1 = 1/sqrt2 and x1 ~ 0.9028 (slope ~2.853, line y = 2.853x - 3.052, PQ ~ 3.739, area ~ 1.632). The key (A,B,C) is the intended reading for the tangent with x1 = 1/sqrt2; for the other tangent (C) would be false. Added the justification, the second-tangent remark and the verdicts on (A) and (D). Answer kept.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the proposed line directly: it is tangent to a curve exactly when the substitution gives a double root.
solution: $f(x)=-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}$ follows from $x=\sin\theta$ and the point $\left(\frac12,-\sqrt3\right)$, so (A) is true.
Put $y=2\sqrt2x-3$ in $x^2=\frac32y$: $x^2-3\sqrt2\,x+\frac92=0$ has discriminant $18-18=0$, so the line touches $C_2$ at $x=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}$, $y=3$: $Q\left(\frac{3\sqrt2}{2},3\right)$.

Put the line in $y=-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}$ and square: $1-x^2=(2\sqrt2x^2-3x)^2\Rightarrow8x^4-12\sqrt2x^3+10x^2-1=0$, which factors as $8\left(x-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^2\left(x^2-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}x-\frac14\right)=0$, with a double root at $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}$.

At $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ the unsquared equation $-\sqrt{1-x^2}=2\sqrt2x^2-3x$ holds (both sides equal $-\frac1{\sqrt2}$), so the line meets $C_1$ with multiplicity two there, i.e. touches $C_1$ at $P\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},-1\right)$. (B) is true.
The line cuts the axes at $\left(\frac{3}{2\sqrt2},0\right)$ and $(0,-3)$; area $=\frac12\cdot\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}\cdot3=\frac{9}{4\sqrt2}$, so (D) is false.

useful_results: The tangent of slope $m$ to $x^2=4ay$ is $y=mx-am^2$; for $x^2=\frac32y$ ($4a=\frac32$) it is $y=mx-\frac{3m^2}{8}$ touching at $x=\frac{3m}{4}$.
Common tangent of two curves: match slope and intercept; equivalently the line substituted into each curve gives a double root.
$\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{1-x^2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}+C$ (use $x=\sin\theta$, $\int\csc^2\theta\,d\theta$). In general $\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{a^2x}$.
Two curves can have more than one common tangent (here also one touching $C_1$ at $x\approx0.903$), so a statement about 'the' common tangent should be checked against every solution.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Chain rule and higher-order derivatives of composite functions
Limits using L'Hôpital's rule
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a twice differentiable function satisfying $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=2$ and $f''(0)=-1$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a composite function defined by $g(x)=f(x+f(x))$. Which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
questions.key_idea: Each limit is $\frac{\varphi''(0)}{2}$ for a composite $\varphi$ with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi'(0)=12$ (or $6$), so only second derivatives at $0$ are needed.
solution: Here $g(0)=f(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=6$, so $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{g(x)-6x}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{g'(x)-6}{2x}=\frac{g''(0)}{2}=-\frac{11}{2}$. Statement (B) is true.
Applying L'Hôpital's rule twice: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(g(x))-12x}{x^2}=\frac{h''(0)}{2}=-29$. Statement (C) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace $f$ by its second-order Taylor polynomial and compose polynomials, discarding $O(x^3)$.

useful_results: If $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi$ is twice differentiable at $0$, then $\varphi(x)=\varphi'(0)x+\frac{\varphi''(0)}{2}x^2+o(x^2)$; so $\lim\frac{\varphi(x)-\varphi'(0)x}{x^2}=\frac{\varphi''(0)}{2}$.
Composition of second-order jets: if $u=ax+bx^2$ and $v=cx+dx^2$ then $u(v(x))=ac\,x+(ad+bc^2)\,x^2$ (check with the chain rule: $(f\circ g)''(0)=f''g'^2+f'g''$).
$(f\circ g)''=f''(g)\,(g')^2+f'(g)\,g''$ — the term $f''(g)(g')^2$ is the one students forget.
Instance: $g=f\circ(\mathrm{id}+f)$ has $g'(0)=6$, $g''(0)=-11$; $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$ have $\varphi'(0)=12$ and $\varphi''(0)=-58$, $-50$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Integration by substitution
Roots of a cubic equation and location of roots
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuously differentiable function such that $f'(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{(x^2+x+1)\sqrt{x^4+x^2+1}}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. If $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=1$, consider the cubic equation $x^3-3x+(f(1)-f(-1))=0$. Which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
options: The equation has three distinct real roots.
The product of all the real roots of the equation is $-\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.
Exactly one real root of the equation lies in the interval $(1,2)$.
Exactly one real root of the equation lies in the interval $(-1,0)$.
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $x^2$ makes the integrand $\frac{du}{(u+1)\sqrt{u^2-1}}$ with $u=x+\frac1x$.
solution: For $x>0$ divide numerator and denominator by $x^2$: $f'(x)=\frac{1-\frac1{x^2}}{\left(x+1+\frac1x\right)\sqrt{x^2+1+\frac1{x^2}}}$.
This derivation used $x>0$; but $F(x)=\sqrt{\frac{x^2-x+1}{x^2+x+1}}$ satisfies $F'(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{(x^2+x+1)\sqrt{x^4+x^2+1}}$ for every real $x$, so $f=F+C$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
The cubic is $x^3-3x-\frac2{\sqrt3}=0$. Let $g(x)=x^3-3x-\frac2{\sqrt3}$; $g'(x)=3(x-1)(x+1)$, with critical points $x=\pm1$.
Local maximum $g(-1)=2-\frac2{\sqrt3}>0$ and local minimum $g(1)=-2-\frac2{\sqrt3}<0$. Since $g(-1)\cdot g(1)<0$, there are three distinct real roots. Statement (A) is true.
The product of the roots is $-\left(-\frac2{\sqrt3}\right)=\frac2{\sqrt3}$, so (B) is false.
Sign changes occur in $(-2,-1)$, $(-1,0)$ and $(1,2)$, one root each. So exactly one root lies in $(-1,0)$ and exactly one in $(1,2)$. Statements (C) and (D) are true.
questions.correction_note: PDF divides numerator and denominator by x^2 and writes sqrt(x^4+x^2+1)/x^... as sqrt(x^2+1+1/x^2); that is valid only for x>0 (for x<0 the root picks up a minus sign), yet the PDF then uses f(-1). The final formula f(x)=sqrt((x^2-x+1)/(x^2+x+1)) is nevertheless correct for all real x because its derivative equals f'(x) everywhere (verified symbolically at several points). Added that justification as one bullet; all values and the answer are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate the guessed antiderivative to confirm it for all real $x$, then solve the cubic in closed form with $x=2\cos\varphi$ and read the roots off.
solution: $\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt R=\frac{R'}{2\sqrt R}=\frac{x^2-1}{(x^2+x+1)^2}\sqrt{\frac{x^2+x+1}{x^2-x+1}}=\frac{x^2-1}{(x^2+x+1)\sqrt{(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)}}$, and $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1)=x^4+x^2+1$. So $f=\sqrt R+C$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and $C=0$.
$\varphi=\frac\alpha3,\ \frac{2\pi-\alpha}3,\ \frac{2\pi+\alpha}3$ give three different values of $\cos\varphi$, hence three distinct real roots $x\approx1.899,\ -0.407,\ -1.492$. (A) is true.
These lie in $(1,2)$, $(-1,0)$ and $(-2,-1)$ respectively: exactly one root in each of $(1,2)$ and $(-1,0)$. (C), (D) are true.
By Vieta the product is $-\left(-\frac2{\sqrt3}\right)=\frac2{\sqrt3}$ ($1.899\times0.407\times1.492\approx1.155$), so (B) is false.

useful_results: For $\int\frac{x^2\pm1}{\text{poly in }x^2,x,\dots}dx$ with palindromic denominators, divide by $x^2$ and use $u=x\mp\frac1x$ (here $x+\frac1x$, $du=(1-\frac1{x^2})dx$).
$\int\frac{du}{(u+1)\sqrt{u^2-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{u-1}{u+1}}+C$ (for $u>1$): check by differentiating, $\frac{d}{du}\sqrt{\frac{u-1}{u+1}}=\frac{1}{(u+1)\sqrt{u^2-1}}$.
$x^3-3x+c=0$ has three distinct real roots iff $|c|<2$; with $x=2\cos\varphi$ it reads $2\cos3\varphi=-c$.
Product of roots of $x^3+px^2+qx+r=0$ is $-r$ (not $+r$); sign-checks at $x=-1,0,1,2$ locate the roots of $x^3-3x+c$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Coaxial system of circles, tangent line and orthogonality of circles
questions.question: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the coaxal system of circles in the Cartesian plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every member of $\mathcal{C}$ is tangent to the $y$-axis at the origin $O(0,0)$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a family of straight lines parameterized by $m\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, defined by the equation $y=mx+\frac1m$. For a fixed line $L\in\mathcal{L}$, let $C_{\lambda_1}$ and $C_{\lambda_2}$ be the two distinct circles in $\mathcal{C}$ that are tangent to $L$, with their centres denoted by $M_1$ and $M_2$ respectively. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the respective points of tangency of $L$ with the circles $C_{\lambda_1}$ and $C_{\lambda_2}$. Which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
options: The length of the line segment $T_1T_2$ is equal to the distance between the parallel lines $M_1T_1$ and $M_2T_2$, and is given by $\frac1{|m|}$.
The circle described with the line segment $T_1T_2$ as a diameter is orthogonal to every member of the coaxal system $\mathcal{C}$.
The length of the line segment $T_1T_2$ is equal to the distance between the parallel lines $M_1T_1$ and $M_2T_2$, and is given by $\frac2{|m|}$.
The area of the right trapezoid formed by the vertices $M_1,T_1,T_2$ and $M_2$ is independent of $m$.
questions.key_idea: The point $P$ where $L$ meets the radical axis (the $y$-axis) has equal tangent lengths $\frac1{|m|}$ to both circles, so $P$ is the midpoint of $T_1T_2$.
solution: Any circle of $\mathcal{C}$ is $C_\lambda:x^2+y^2-2\lambda x=0$, with centre $M(\lambda,0)$ and radius $|\lambda|$.

The roots $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ give the centres $M_1(\lambda_1,0)$, $M_2(\lambda_2,0)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=2$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2=-\frac1{m^2}<0$ (centres on opposite sides of $O$); the midpoint of $M_1M_2$ is $(1,0)$.
The radical axis of $\mathcal{C}$ is the $y$-axis ($x=0$); it meets $L$ at $P\left(0,\frac1m\right)$.
Power of $P$ with respect to either circle: $0^2+\left(\frac1m\right)^2-2\lambda(0)=\frac1{m^2}$, so the tangent lengths are $PT_1=PT_2=\frac1{|m|}$.

As $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$, $T_1$ and $T_2$ lie on opposite sides of $P$ on $L$. So $P\left(0,\frac1m\right)$ is the midpoint of $T_1T_2$, and the circle on $T_1T_2$ as diameter has radius $\frac1{|m|}$.

This circle is tangent to the $x$-axis at the origin, while every $C_\lambda$ is tangent to the $y$-axis at the origin; the tangents at the common point $O$ are perpendicular, so the circles are orthogonal to every member of $\mathcal{C}$. Statement (B) is true.
$M_1T_1$ and $M_2T_2$ are both perpendicular to $L$, hence parallel to each other.
$T_1T_2$ acts as the perpendicular distance between them: $T_1T_2=PT_1+PT_2=\frac2{|m|}$. Statement (C) is true and (A) is false.
Area of the right trapezoid $M_1T_1T_2M_2$ $=\frac12(R_1+R_2)\,(T_1T_2)$, with $R_1+R_2=|\lambda_1|+|\lambda_2|=|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|=\sqrt{4+\frac4{m^2}}=\frac{2\sqrt{m^2+1}}{|m|}$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{m^2+1}}{|m|}\cdot\frac2{|m|}=\frac{2\sqrt{m^2+1}}{m^2}$, which depends on $m$. Statement (D) is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: A circle centred on the radical axis with radius equal to the tangent length is orthogonal to the whole coaxal system; and $T_1T_2$ is the projection of $M_1M_2$ on $L$.
solution: The $y$-axis is the radical axis of the system, so $P=L\cap(y\text{-axis})=\left(0,\frac1m\right)$ has the same power $p=\frac1{m^2}$ with respect to every circle of $\mathcal{C}$.

A circle with centre $P$ and radius$^2$ equal to $p$ is orthogonal to a circle with centre $M$ and radius $r$ because $PM^2=r^2+p$ (power of $P$). So the circle with centre $P$ and radius $\frac1{|m|}$, which is the circle on $T_1T_2$ as diameter, is orthogonal to every member. (B) is true.
$T_1T_2$ is the distance between the parallel lines $M_1T_1,M_2T_2$, i.e. the projection of $M_1M_2$ on $L$: $T_1T_2=|M_1M_2|\cos\varphi$ where $\varphi$ is the angle between $L$ and the $x$-axis.

Area of the trapezoid $=\frac12(R_1+R_2)T_1T_2=\frac12\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{m^2+1}}{|m|}\cdot\frac2{|m|}=\frac{2\sqrt{m^2+1}}{m^2}$: depends on $m$ (for instance $m=1$ gives $2\sqrt2$ and $m=2$ gives $\frac{\sqrt5}{2}$). (D) is false.

useful_results: For circles $x^2+y^2-2\lambda x=0$ touching the $y$-axis at $O$, the radical axis is $x=0$; the power of any point $(0,t)$ is $t^2$ for every member.
A line tangent to two circles of a coaxal system meets the radical axis at the midpoint of the two points of contact (equal tangent lengths).

A circle with centre on the radical axis and radius $=\sqrt{\text{power of the centre}}$ is orthogonal to all members of the coaxal system; two circles through $O$ whose tangents at $O$ are perpendicular are orthogonal.
Tangency of $y=mx+\frac1m$ to $x^2+y^2-2\lambda x=0$ gives $\lambda^2-2\lambda-\frac1{m^2}=0$, so $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=2$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2=-\frac1{m^2}<0$ for every $m$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Properties of definite integrals: King property
questions.question: Consider the following definite integrals: $I_1=\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)}{1+\cos2x+\sqrt3\sin2x}\,dx$, $I_2=\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{x}{1+\cos2x+\sqrt3\sin2x}\,dx$ and $I_3=\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{\cos\left(2x-\frac\pi3\right)\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)}{1+\cos2x+\sqrt3\sin2x}\,dx$. Which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
questions.key_idea: The denominator is unchanged under $x\to\frac\pi3-x$, while $\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)$ turns into $\ln4-\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)$.
solution: Reflection $x\to\frac\pi3-x$: $2x-\frac\pi3\to-\left(2x-\frac\pi3\right)$, and $\cos$ is even, so $D(x)$ is invariant.
Under the reflection the numerator of $I_1$ becomes $\ln\left(1+\sqrt3\tan\left(\frac\pi3-x\right)\right)=\ln\left(1+\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3-\tan x}{1+\sqrt3\tan x}\right)=\ln4-\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)$.

For $I_2$, the reflection gives $I_2=\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{\frac\pi3-x}{D(x)}dx=\frac\pi3J-I_2$, so $2I_2=\frac\pi3\cdot\frac{\ln2}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow I_2=\frac{\pi\ln2}{6\sqrt3}$. Statement (B) is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $u=1+\sqrt3\tan x$ so that $\frac{dx}{D}=\frac{du}{2\sqrt3\,u}$; and write $\cos\left(2x-\frac\pi3\right)=\frac{D-1}{2}$.
solution: The part with $\theta$ is odd and integrates to zero, leaving $I_2=\frac\pi{12}\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\frac{d\theta}{1+2\cos\theta}=\frac\pi{12}\cdot\frac{2\ln2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi\ln2}{6\sqrt3}$. (B) is false.
Let $K=\int_0^{\pi/3}\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x)dx$. The reflection $x\to\frac\pi3-x$ gives $K=\int_0^{\pi/3}(\ln4-\ln(1+\sqrt3\tan x))dx=\frac\pi3\ln4-K$, so $K=\frac{\pi\ln2}{3}$.
$I_3=\frac{\pi\ln2}{6}-\frac{(\ln2)^2}{2\sqrt3}$. (C) is true; and $I_1+3I_2=\frac{\ln2}{\sqrt3}\left(\ln2+\frac\pi2\right)$, so (D) is true.

useful_results: King-type reflection $x\to a+b-x$ works whenever the denominator is invariant and the numerator turns into (constant) $-$ (itself): $\int f=\frac{\text{constant}}{2}\int\frac1D$.

$1+\sqrt3\tan\left(\frac\pi3-x\right)=\frac{4}{1+\sqrt3\tan x}$; in general $(1+\tan a\tan x)\bigl(1+\tan a\tan(a'-x)\bigr)$ is constant when $a'$ is the complementary angle: $(1+\tan x)(1+\tan(\frac\pi4-x))=2$.
$\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{d\theta}{1+2\cos\theta}=\frac{\ln2}{\sqrt3}$ and, with $\theta\in(-\frac\pi3,\frac\pi3)$, odd-times-even terms vanish.
$1+\cos2x+\sqrt3\sin2x=2\cos^2x\,(1+\sqrt3\tan x)=1+2\cos\left(2x-\frac\pi3\right)$: rewriting $a\cos2x+b\sin2x$ as one cosine exposes the symmetry.

concepts: Definite integrals: Wallis' formula and reduction formulas
questions.question:
Match the definite integrals in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II.
List-I: (P) $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^6x\,dx$; (Q) $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4x\cos^2x\,dx$; (R) $\int_0^1x^2\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$; (S) $\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^4x\,dx$.
List-II: (1) $\frac{\pi}{32}$; (2) $\frac{5\pi}{32}$; (3) $\frac{\pi}{16}$; (4) $\frac\pi4-\frac23$; (5) $\frac{3\pi}{16}$.
questions.key_idea: Wallis' formula for $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^m\cos^n$, and the reduction $T_n+T_{n-2}=\frac1{n-1}$ for $\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n$.
solution: Hence P→2, Q→1, R→3, S→4, which is option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the Beta function $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^a\theta\cos^b\theta\,d\theta=\frac12B\left(\frac{a+1}2,\frac{b+1}2\right)$, and for (S) write $\tan^4=\tan^2(\sec^2-1)$.

useful_results: Wallis: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^m x\cos^n x\,dx=\frac{(m-1)!!\,(n-1)!!}{(m+n)!!}\cdot\kappa$ with $\kappa=\frac\pi2$ if $m,n$ are both even and $\kappa=1$ otherwise.
Beta form: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^a\cos^b=\frac12B\left(\frac{a+1}2,\frac{b+1}2\right)$; and $\int_0^1x^{p}\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$ becomes a Wallis integral by $x=\sin\theta$.
$\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^nx\,dx=\frac{1}{n-1}-\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\,dx$ for $n\ge2$, with $T_0=\frac\pi4$ and $T_1=\frac{\ln2}{2}$.
Quick elimination: only (S) involves $\frac\pi4-\frac23$ ($\approx0.118$), and $\frac{5\pi}{32}>\frac{\pi}{16}>\frac{\pi}{32}$ settles P, Q, R by size.

concepts: Image (reflection) of a point and of a line
Orthogonal circles and a tangent line to a circle
questions.question:
Match the statements in List-I with their corresponding values in List-II.
List-I: (P) Let $C_1$ be the circle $x^2+y^2-2x-4y+1=0$. If the image of the centre of $C_1$ with respect to the line $x+y-1=0$ is the centre of a circle $C_2$ which cuts $C_1$ orthogonally, then the square of the radius of $C_2$ is equal to; (Q) Let the image of the line $x-2y+4=0$ with respect to the line $x-y+1=0$ be the line $L$. If a circle $C_3$ with centre $(1,6)$ touches the line $L$, then the square of the radius of $C_3$ is equal to; (R) A circle $C_4$ passes through the origin and its centre lies at the image of the point $(3,4)$ with respect to the line $x=0$. If $C_4$ cuts the circle $x^2+y^2-2x-2y+k=0$ orthogonally, then the value of $k$ is equal to; (S) Let the image of the point $(4,3)$ with respect to the line $x+y-1=0$ be the centre of a circle $C_7$. If $C_7$ cuts the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ orthogonally, then the square of the radius of $C_7$ is equal to.
List-II: (1) $4$; (2) $5$; (3) $2$; (4) $9$; (5) $3$.
questions.key_idea: Orthogonality of two circles means $d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2$ (centres at distance $d$), and an image is found with the reflection formula.
solution: The point $(0,2)$ on $x-2y+4=0$ has image $(1,1)$ in $x-y+1=0$.
So $L$ passes through $(2,3)$ and $(1,1)$; its equation is $2x-y-1=0$.
The radius of $C_3$ is the perpendicular distance from $(1,6)$ to $L$: $r_3=\frac{|2(1)-6-1|}{\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}}=\sqrt5$, so $r_3^2=5$. (Q)$\to$(2).
(R) The image of $(3,4)$ in $x=0$ is $(-3,4)$, the centre of $C_4$; it passes through $(0,0)$, so $r_4^2=(-3)^2+4^2=25$.
The other circle has centre $(1,1)$ and $r_5^2=1+1-k=2-k$. The square of the distance between the centres is $d^2=(-3-1)^2+(4-1)^2=25$.
(S) The image of $(4,3)$ in $x+y-1=0$ is $(-2,-3)$, the centre of $C_7$. Its distance squared from the origin is $d^2=(-2)^2+(-3)^2=13$.
Hence P→1, Q→2, R→3, S→4, which is option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflections preserve distances, so for (Q) reflect the centre instead of the line; and use the general-form condition $2g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_2$ for orthogonality.
solution: (Q) A circle touching the reflected line $L$ with centre $(1,6)$ has the same radius as the circle touching $x-2y+4=0$ whose centre is the mirror image of $(1,6)$ in $x-y+1=0$.
The image of $(1,6)$: value of $x-y+1$ is $-4$, so the image is $(1,6)-(-4)(1,-1)=(5,2)$.
Distance from $(5,2)$ to $x-2y+4=0$: $\frac{|5-4+4|}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5$, so $r_3^2=5$ (no need to find $L$). (Q)$\to$(2).

useful_results: Circles $(g_1,f_1,c_1)$ and $(g_2,f_2,c_2)$ are orthogonal iff $2g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_2$, equivalently $d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2$.
A reflection is an isometry: tangency, distances and radii of circles touching a line are unchanged if the line and the centre are reflected together.
An orthogonal circle about a point $C$ with centre at distance $d$ from the centre of a given circle of radius $r$ has $r_2^2=d^2-r^2=$ power of $C$ w.r.t. the given circle (here $13-4=9$).

concepts: Properties of definite integrals
Intermediate value theorem and Rolle's theorem
questions.question: Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function which is not identically zero on $[0,1]$. Consider a real-valued function $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $g(t)=\int_0^1e^{tx}f(x)\,dx$. If $g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=0$, then the minimum possible number of distinct roots of the equation $f(x)=0$ in the open interval $(0,1)$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: $\int_0^1f=0$ and $\int_0^1xf=0$ give $\int_0^1(x-c)f(x)\,dx=0$ for every $c$, so $f$ cannot change sign only once.
solution: Differentiating under the integral sign and putting $t=0$: $g(0)=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx=0$ and $g'(0)=\int_0^1xf(x)\,dx=0$.
$f$ is continuous, not identically zero, and $\int_0^1f=0$, so it takes both positive and negative values on $(0,1)$.
By the Intermediate Value Theorem, $f$ has at least one root in $(0,1)$.
Suppose $f$ has exactly one root $c\in(0,1)$, where it changes sign.
Then $h(x)=(x-c)f(x)$ does not change sign on $(0,1)$ and is not identically zero, so $\int_0^1(x-c)f(x)\,dx\neq0$.
So $f$ must have at least $2$ distinct roots in $(0,1)$.
Its roots are $x=\frac12\pm\frac1{2\sqrt3}$, both in $(0,1)$. The minimum number is $2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Integrate once: $F(x)=\int_0^xf$ has $F(0)=F(1)=0$ and, by parts, $\int_0^1F=0$; then Rolle's theorem is used twice.
solution: $F\not\equiv0$ (else $f=F'\equiv0$), $F$ is continuous and $\int_0^1F=0$, so $F$ takes both signs on $(0,1)$ and, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, vanishes at some $a\in(0,1)$.
Now $F(0)=F(a)=F(1)=0$; Rolle's theorem on $[0,a]$ and $[a,1]$ gives $f=F'$ zeros in $(0,a)$ and in $(a,1)$ — two distinct roots in $(0,1)$.
The example $f(x)=x^2-x+\frac16$ has exactly two roots, so the minimum is $2$.

useful_results: If $\int_0^1f=0$ and $\int_0^1xf=0$ ($f$ continuous, $\not\equiv0$) then $f$ is orthogonal to all polynomials of degree $\le1$ and has at least $2$ sign changes; in general, $\int_0^1x^kf=0$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$ forces at least $n$ zeros in $(0,1)$.
Repeated integration: if $F_1=\int_0^xf$ and $F_2=\int_0^xF_1$, orthogonality to $1,x,\dots,x^{n-1}$ means $F_n$ vanishes to order $n$ at both ends, so Rolle's theorem gives the zeros of $f$.
The Legendre-type example: $x^2-x+\frac16$ (shifted Legendre $P_2$ scaled) is orthogonal to $1,x$ on $[0,1]$ and has exactly $2$ roots, so the bound is sharp.
$\frac{d}{dt}\int_0^1e^{tx}f(x)\,dx\Big|_{t=0}=\int_0^1xf(x)\,dx$: differentiating $g$ at $0$ produces the moments of $f$.

concepts: Indefinite integration: integration by parts and recurrence relations
questions.question: Let $C^\infty(0,\infty)$ denote the vector space of all infinitely differentiable real-valued functions defined on the interval $(0,\infty)$. For a given function $f\in C^\infty(0,\infty)$, a sequence of functions $\{f_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ is generated recursively: $f_0(x)=f(x)$ and $f_{n+1}(x)=x\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(f_n(x)\bigr)+nf_n(x)$ for all $n\ge0$ and $x>0$. If the indefinite integral of the function $f_5(x)$ with respect to $x$ is expressed in the form $\int f_5(x)\,dx=x\sum_{k=1}^{4}c_kf_k(x)+C$, where $c_k$ ($k=1,2,3,4$) are real constants independent of the choice of $f$, and $C$ is the arbitrary constant of integration, then the value of $c_3$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: Integrating $x^{k-1}f_{n+1}$ by parts gives the reduction $\int x^{k-1}f_{n+1}=x^kf_n+(n-k)\int x^{k-1}f_n$; take $k=1$.
solution: By parts on the first term, with $x^k$ first and $f_n'$ second: $\int x^kf_n'(x)\,dx=x^kf_n(x)-k\int x^{k-1}f_n(x)\,dx$.
For $\int f_5\,dx$ take $k=1$ and $n=4$: $\int f_5\,dx=xf_4+3\int f_4\,dx$.
Applying the relation for $n=3,2,1$ with $k=1$: $\int f_4\,dx=xf_3+2\int f_3\,dx$; $\int f_3\,dx=xf_2+1\cdot\int f_2\,dx$; $\int f_2\,dx=xf_1+0=xf_1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since the $c_k$ do not depend on $f$, test the identity on $f=x^p$, where $f_n=(p)_n\,x^p$ with rising factorials, and compare polynomials in $p$.
solution: So $c_3=3$ (and $(c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)=(6,6,3,1)$ as in the main solution).

useful_results: The operator $f\mapsto xf'+nf$ is $(xD+n)$; on $x^p$ it multiplies by $(p+n)$, so $f_n=(xD)(xD+1)\cdots$ acts on $x^p$ as $(p)_n$. Testing monomials determines constants that are independent of $f$.
Integration by parts reduction: $\int x^{k-1}\bigl(xf'+nf\bigr)dx=x^kf+(n-k)\int x^{k-1}f\,dx$; the coefficient $n-k$ vanishes when $n=k$, which ends the recursion.
The recursion stops at $f_2$ because $f_2=xf_1'+f_1\cdot1$ with $n=1$ gives $f_2=(xf_1)'$, hence $\int f_2\,dx=xf_1$ exactly.
Check: $f=1$ gives $f_1=0$, so all $f_k=0$ and both sides vanish; $f=x$ gives $f_n=(1)_nx=n!\,x$ and $\int f_5=60x^2$, while $x\sum c_kk!x=x^2(6+12+18+24)=60x^2$.

concepts: Rolle's theorem and absolute extrema on a closed interval
questions.question: Consider the function $f:[1,4]\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x$. Let $c\in(1,4)$ be the value that satisfies Rolle's theorem for $f(x)$ on the interval $[1,4]$. If $M$ and $m$ denote the greatest and the least values of $f(x)$ on $[1,4]$ respectively, then the value of $M-m+c$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: $f(1)=f(4)$, so Rolle's theorem applies and $c$ is the critical point $x=2$, which is also where the maximum occurs.
solution: At the endpoints $f(1)=1-9+24=16$ and $f(4)=64-144+96=16$. Since $f(1)=f(4)$, Rolle's theorem is applicable.
Evaluate $f$ at the critical points and endpoints: $f(1)=16$, $f(2)=8-36+48=20$, $f(4)=16$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Factorise $f(x)-16$ and $f(x)-20$ to see the extreme values and where they occur without any table.
solution: $f(x)-20=x^3-9x^2+24x-20=(x-2)^2(x-5)\le0$ on $[1,4]$ since $x-5<0$, so $f\le20$ with equality at $x=2$. Thus $M=20$.
The repeated factors $(x-4)^2$ and $(x-2)^2$ show $f'(4)=f'(2)=0$, so Rolle's point in $(1,4)$ is $c=2$.

useful_results: For a cubic with $f(a)=f(b)$, Rolle's point $c$ solves $f'(c)=0$ in $(a,b)$; here $f'=3(x-2)(x-4)$ has the roots $2\in(1,4)$ and $4\notin(1,4)$.
A cubic takes the value $v$ with a double root exactly when $v$ is a local extreme value: $f-20=(x-2)^2(x-5)$ and $f-16=(x-1)(x-4)^2$ show the local maximum $20$ and minimum $16$ at once.
On a closed interval check the endpoints as well as the critical points: here $f(1)=16=f(4)$ equals the local minimum value, so the minimum is attained at both endpoints.
Sum of the roots of $f'(x)=0$ is $6$ and $f$ is symmetric about the inflection point $x=3$ (since $f''(3)=0$): $f(2)+f(4)=36=2f(3)$.

concepts: Monotonicity of a function
Quadratic inequality valid for all real $x$
questions.question: Consider a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=(a^2-1)x^3+3(a-1)x^2+6x+7$ where $a\in\mathbb{R}$. If $f(x)$ is monotonically increasing for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then the number of integral values of $a$ in the interval $[-5,5]$ is ____.
questions.key_idea: A cubic is increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ iff $f'(x)\ge0$ for all $x$; the degenerate case $a^2-1=0$ must be treated separately.
solution: $f$ is monotonically increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ iff $f'(x)\ge0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
For $a=1$ the inequality becomes $2\ge0$, which is always true, so $a=1$ is valid.
For $a=-1$ it becomes $-4x+2\ge0$, which does not hold for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, so $a=-1$ is rejected.
Case 2: $a^2-1\neq0$. The quadratic is non-negative for all $x$ iff the coefficient of $x^2$ is positive and the discriminant $D\le0$.
The intersection of the two conditions gives $a\le-3$ or $a>1$.
Integers in $[-5,5]$: $-5,-4,-3$ and $1,2,3,4,5$, which is $3+5=8$ values.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square: for $a^2>1$ the minimum of the quadratic is at its vertex, and its value $\frac{a+3}{a+1}$ decides the sign (a vertex view in place of the discriminant).
solution: For $a^2>1$ (so the parabola opens upward) the minimum is at $x=-\frac{a-1}{a^2-1}=-\frac1{a+1}$.
Need $\frac{a+3}{a+1}\ge0\Rightarrow a\le-3$ or $a>-1$; with $a^2>1$ this means $a\le-3$ or $a>1$. For $a^2<1$ the parabola opens downward and cannot stay non-negative.

useful_results: $f$ is non-decreasing on $\mathbb{R}$ iff $f'\ge0$ everywhere; if $f'$ is zero only at isolated points $f$ is still strictly increasing.
$Ax^2+Bx+C\ge0$ for all real $x$ iff ($A>0,\ B^2-4AC\le0$) or ($A=0,\ B=0,\ C\ge0$). Always handle $A=0$ separately when the leading coefficient carries a parameter.
Vertex form: for $A>0$ the minimum value is $C-\frac{B^2}{4A}=-\frac{D}{4A}$; here $\frac{a+3}{a+1}$.
Instance: $(a^2-1)x^2+2(a-1)x+2$ has $\frac D4=-(a-1)(a+3)$, so it stays non-negative for $a\in(-\infty,-3]\cup[1,\infty)$ (with $a=-1$ excluded).

concepts: Differentiability of greatest integer and fractional part functions
Derivative of a function with respect to another function
questions.question: Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ and $\{x\}$ denote the greatest integer function and the fractional part function of $x$, respectively. Let $m$ be the number of points in the interval $(0,2)$ where the function $h(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor+\left|\{x\}-\frac12\right|$ is not differentiable. Consider two functions defined in the interval $(1,2)$ as $u(x)=\ln(1+\{x\})$ and $v(x)=\frac{1}{1-\{x\}}$. If $d$ is the value of the derivative of $u(x)$ with respect to $v(x)$ at $x=\frac32$, then the value of $\frac md$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: $h$ has a corner at each half-integer and a jump at each integer, so in $(0,2)$ the non-differentiable points are $\frac12,1,\frac32$.
solution: For $x\in(0,1)$: $\lfloor x\rfloor=0$ and $\{x\}=x$, so $h(x)=\left|x-\frac12\right|$, which is non-differentiable at the corner point $x=\frac12$.
$h$ is discontinuous at $x=1$, hence not differentiable there.
For $x\in(1,2)$: $\lfloor x\rfloor=1$ and $\{x\}=x-1$, so $h(x)=1+\left|x-\frac32\right|$, non-differentiable at the corner point $x=\frac32$.
The points of non-differentiability in $(0,2)$ are $x=\frac12,1,\frac32$, so $m=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express $v$ as a function of $u$ by eliminating $x$ (so $\frac{dv}{du}$ is read off at once), and read the graph of $h$ as a zigzag in each unit cell.
solution: $h(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor+\left|x-\left(\lfloor x\rfloor+\tfrac12\right)\right|$: on each cell $[n,n+1)$ it is a V-shape with vertex $\left(n+\frac12,\,n\right)$ and end heights $n+\frac12$; the next cell starts at height $n+\frac32$, so there is a jump of $1$ at every integer.
So in $(0,2)$ the vertices (corners) are at $\frac12$ and $\frac32$, and at the integer $x=1$ the left limit $\frac12$ differs from the right limit $\frac32$ (a jump of $1$). Hence $m=3$.

useful_results: For $h=\lfloor x\rfloor+g(\{x\})$ with $g$ continuous on $[0,1]$: $h$ is continuous at the integers iff $g(1)-g(0)=1$ (for example $g(t)=t$ gives $h=x$). Here $g(t)=\left|t-\frac12\right|$ has $g(1)-g(0)=0\neq1$, so every integer is a jump.
$|\{x\}-\frac12|$ has corners at $x=n+\frac12$ (and nowhere else); each integer adds one more non-differentiable point because of the jump.
Derivative of $u$ with respect to $v$: $\frac{du}{dv}=\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}$ wherever $v'\ne0$.
Within $(n,n+1)$ the functions $\lfloor x\rfloor$ and $\{x\}=x-n$ are smooth, so substitute $\{x\}=x-n$ before differentiating.

concepts: Length of tangent and normal to a curve
Differential equations: variable separable
questions.question: Let $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be a differentiable function representing a curve $y=f(x)$. Let $T$ and $N$ denote the length of the tangent and the length of the normal to the curve at any point $P(x,y)$ on it, respectively. Suppose that $f'(x)>0$ for all $x>0$ and the function satisfies the relation $\frac1y\left(\frac NT\right)=x+\frac1x$ for all $x>0$. If $f(2)=2e^2$, then the value of $\ln\left(\frac{f(4)}{4}\right)$ is equal to ____.
questions.key_idea: $\frac NT=\frac{dy}{dx}$, so the relation is the separable equation $\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=x+\frac1x$.
solution: For $y=f(x)$ the length of the normal and of the tangent at $P(x,y)$ are $N=\left|y\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}\right|$ and $T=\left|\frac{y\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}}{\frac{dy}{dx}}\right|$.
So the curve is $\ln y=\frac{x^2}{2}+\ln x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $N/T=\tan\psi$ from the right triangle formed by the tangent, the normal and the $x$-axis, and the quantity asked is already $\ln\frac yx$, so integrate that directly.
solution: The tangent and the normal at $P$ meet the $x$-axis at $A$ and $B$; $PA=T$, $PB=N$ and $\angle APB=90^\circ$. The angle at $A$ is the inclination $\psi$ of the tangent, so $\tan\psi=\frac{PB}{PA}=\frac NT$.

useful_results: For $y=f(x)$: tangent length $T=\left|\frac{y}{y'}\sqrt{1+y'^2}\right|$, normal length $N=|y|\sqrt{1+y'^2}$, sub-tangent $\left|\frac{y}{y'}\right|$, sub-normal $|yy'|$; hence $\frac NT=|y'|$.
A relation of the form $\frac{y'}{y}=p(x)$ gives $y=Ce^{\int p\,dx}$; here $y=x\,e^{x^2/2}$ (check: $f(2)=2e^2$).
Combine $\ln y-\ln x$ when the question asks for $\ln\frac yx$: $\frac{d}{dx}\ln\frac yx=\frac{y'}{y}-\frac1x$.
Always check the constant of integration with the given point; here $C=0$ since $\ln(2e^2)=\ln2+2$.
